title: The nine treasures
hook: remember Guru Tegh Bahadur and the nine treasures come running home

segments.voice: Yesterday: Har Rai and Har Krishan, and your line: all pain goes. Did you sit with someone who was hurting? Today the Ardas reaches the ninth Guru, the one we spent a month with. Day six hundred eighteen.
screen: `HAR RAI AND HAR KRISHAN — ALL PAIN GOES.`

segments.voice: There's a strange thing in this line of the Ardas, and once you see it, it's hard to unsee. For the past month we read Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks: the world is a dream, nothing stays, strength gone, all companions gone. And we know how his life ended: arrested, imprisoned, executed in Delhi. By any ordinary measure, he lost everything the world can take. And yet, when the Ardas reaches his name, it promises the opposite of loss. Remember him, it says, and every kind of treasure comes running to your house. How does the man who lost everything become the one who brings everything home? Today: the nine treasures.
screen: `A MONTH OF NOTHING STAYS.` → `HE LOST EVERYTHING THE WORLD TAKES.` → `AND THE ARDAS PROMISES TREASURE.`

segments.voice: The line is: tegh bahaadar simariai, ghar nau nidh aavai dhaai. Remember Tegh Bahadur, and the nine treasures come running home. Nau is nine. Nidh is a treasure, a store of wealth. In old Indian lore, the nine treasures belonged to the god of riches: nine kinds of fabulous wealth, everything a person could want. In ordinary use, nau nidh can stand for every good thing at once. And notice the verb: aavai dhaai, comes running. Not trickles in. Runs, like a child to the door. But Gurbani does something interesting with this phrase. The Sukhmani Sahib, for one, says the nine treasures are the Name of God: whoever has the Name lacks nothing. So the promise in the Ardas works on two levels. On the plain level, Sikhs ask that remembering the ninth Guru bring blessing to their homes. On the deeper level, it echoes his own saloks. What did the last salok say? I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it. The man who lost everything the world can take was holding the one treasure it can't. Remember him, and you remember that. Remember, too, his name. He was born Tyag Mal; tradition says he was given the name Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword, after fighting bravely as a young man beside his father, Guru Hargobind. Brave of the sword, and yet remembered for the treasure he held in his heart. That's the paradox the Ardas sets in one line: the poorest-looking moment, and the richest.
screen: `NAU NIDH: THE NINE TREASURES.` · `AAVAI DHAAI: THEY COME RUNNING.` · `THE REAL TREASURE IS THE NAME.` · `TYAG MAL, BRAVE OF THE SWORD.` · then, large: `NINE TREASURES HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a home full of treasures. Sit and breathe. Picture your home, or a home you love. Then fill it, slowly, but not with money. Put in it the treasures that would actually make it rich: a laugh at the dinner table, someone who listens, a quiet morning, a faith or a hope, a friend who drops by. Name each one as it arrives. Notice which ones are already there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, as the one treasure Gurbani says holds the rest. The bell holds the time.
The nine treasures. Nau nidh: every good thing, and in Gurbani, the Name; remember the ninth Guru, and they come running home.
Your line: nine treasures home. Tonight, name one treasure in your home that money didn't buy, out loud, to someone who's part of it. Day six hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs say that remembering Guru Tegh Bahadur brings the nine treasures running home, and Gurbani often names the Name of God as the true nine treasures.

options: that loss is coming for everyone.
that remembering him brings the nine treasures running home.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nau nidh, the nine treasures; every good thing, and in Gurbani, often the Name itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: the nine treasures is a promise of wealth.
what it means: on the deeper level, it's the Name, the one treasure the ninth Guru held when he lost the rest.
what a scholar hears: nau nidhi recalls the nine treasures of Kubera in Indian lore; Gurbani repeatedly equates them with naam.

notes: Line tegh bahaadar simariai ghar nau nidh aavai dhaai: confirm.
Gurbani lines equating the Name with nau nidh (e.g. 'nau nidh amrit prabh ka naam', Sukhmani): add a precise Ang.
Tyag Mal and the naming after the battle at Kartarpur (1635): traditional; confirm.
Nine treasures of Kubera: confirm the link is stated fairly.
